title: How to Control a Riot
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the WKRP in Cincinnati episode modeled on the 1979 Who concert stampede in Cincinnati, then turn to crowd behavior and riot control. They cover mob mentality and anonymity, the fuel-and-spark model of riots (including the "shilling incident" idea), police crowd-management tactics (the square formation, echelons, command and arrest teams), less-lethal weapons (batons, beanbag, sponge and blunt-force rounds, pepper balls, tear gas, Taser shock wave, dye markers), and prevention through permits and negotiation. Historical examples include the 1992 Los Angeles riots, the 1886 Haymarket riot, the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, the 1943 Detroit riot, the Seattle WTO protests, and recent unrest in Tunisia and Moscow. The episode closes with listener Facebook questions.

segments.title: Opening banter and WKRP stampede story
segments.summary: Hosts chat about a Marc Maron show and WKRP in Cincinnati, then discuss the real Cincinnati stampede at a Who concert where general admission crowds were trampled.

segments.title: Crowd behavior, mob mentality and anonymity
segments.summary: The hosts define crowd behavior and mob mentality, cite Black Friday stampedes, and explain how anonymity within a crowd makes people act in ways they otherwise would not.

segments.title: Fuel and spark theory of riots
segments.summary: Riots are described as needing fuel, built-up grievances such as the LA police and racial prejudice, and a spark, which can be a rumor. The shilling incident is introduced as the signal that tips a crowd into rioting.

segments.title: Police formations and the tactical square
segments.summary: Past police tactics of direct confrontation are contrasted with the modern approach. The hosts describe the tactical square with a command team, arrest team, and echelons of about ten to twelve officers, which can move and reposition and lets people leave.

segments.title: Less-lethal weapons and rounds
segments.summary: Equipment includes riot helmets, shields, body armor, and batons. Less-lethal options include blunt-force rounds, beanbag rounds, sponge rounds, pepper ball rounds, Taser shock wave barricades, and tear gas. Dye markers help identify targets for later arrest. Dogs and horses are used, and animals are relatively immune to tear gas.

segments.title: Prevention, permits and police intimidation
segments.summary: Police aim to prevent riots by negotiating with organizers and issuing permits. The Seattle WTO protests are cited as an example of poor preparation. Police are meant to stay unbiased and show authority, using intimidation such as banging batons on shields when a riot starts.

segments.title: Police riots and historical examples
segments.summary: The hosts discuss police riots, focusing on the 1886 Haymarket riot in Chicago, including the bombing, the shootings, and the trial of anarchists. They also cover the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, the Chicago Ten film, and the 1943 Detroit riot sparked by rumors.

segments.title: Modern unrest in Tunisia and Moscow
segments.summary: The hosts mention race riots in Moscow and anti-government unrest in Tunisia, sparked by a street vendor's self-immolation, which spread through Facebook. Anonymous reportedly urged the Tunisian government to open up the internet.

segments.title: Facebook questions and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts answer listener questions about dream jobs, cheese versus movies, favorite beers, childhood toys, coffee intake, and the recording studio. They close by directing listeners to How Stuff Works for more on riot control.
